Lutheran Worship
LOO-ther-an WUR-ship
noun / doctrine
From Martin Luther, the German reformer whose recovery of the gospel shaped the worship of the churches that bear his name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Lutheran worship is the worship of the churches gathered upon the teaching of Martin Luther, the reformer through whom God in 1517 began to call His church back to the gospel of justification by faith alone. The dictionary honours much in Luther’s recovery: he tore down the false sacrifice of the Mass, restored the cup to the people, set the preaching of the word at the centre, gave the Scriptures to the common man in his own tongue, and filled the church again with congregational hymn-singing, that the whole people might praise God with understanding. For these mercies the church is forever in his debt. Yet Lutheran worship retained corruptions the further Reformation cast off. In the Supper it confessed consubstantiation, a sacramental union in which the body and blood of Christ are held to be present in, with, and under the bread and wine, against the Reformed reading of Christ’s words, “this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24–26). And in worship it kept the “normative principle,” permitting whatever Scripture does not forbid — retaining altars, images, candles, and ceremonies — against the regulative principle, that God may be worshipped only as He has commanded. The Lord saith, “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto” (Deu 12:32), and forbids the graven image and the worshipping of God by men’s devices (Exo 20:4–5). True worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The worship of the Lutheran churches, honoured for Luther's gospel recovery but corrupted by consubstantiation and the normative principle.

expand to see more

LUTHERAN WORSHIP, the worship of the churches founded on Luther's teaching.

It rightly recovered justification by faith and the preaching of the word.

It restored congregational hymn-singing and the Scriptures in the common tongue.

Yet it confessed consubstantiation, a sacramental union in the Supper.

And it kept the normative principle, retaining altars, images, and ceremonies.

📖 Key Scripture

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Deu 12:32 — "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it."

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

1Co 11:24 — "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Honoured for Luther's gospel recovery, Lutheran worship is corrupted by consubstantiation in the Supper and the normative principle against the regulative.

expand to see more

The corruption in Lutheran worship is twofold, and the dictionary names it as error, not difference. First, in the Lord’s Supper, Lutheranism confessed consubstantiation, the sacramental union, holding that the very body and blood of Christ are present in, with, and under the bread and wine, received by the mouth of all communicants. This corrupts the Supper, which is a memorial sign-and-seal wherein Christ is spiritually present to the believer by faith; the Lord said “this do in remembrance of me,” and His glorified body is in heaven, not enclosed in the elements upon ten thousand altars.

Second, Lutheran worship kept the normative principle, the rule that whatever Scripture does not expressly forbid may be retained in worship; and so it kept altars, crucifixes, images, vestments, and ceremonies inherited from Rome. Against this stands the regulative principle, the great recovery of the Reformed and Puritan church: that God may be worshipped only in the ways He has appointed, for what He has not commanded in His worship He has forbidden. “Thou shalt not add thereto” (Deu 12:32). Luther swept much filth from the church; it remained for the further Reformation to sweep the rest, and to worship the Father in spirit and in truth, after His command alone.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Named from Martin Luther, whose gospel recovery shaped the worship of the churches that bear his name.

expand to see more

Lutheran — from Martin Luther, the German reformer.

Luther recovered justification by faith alone in 1517.

He restored congregational hymn-singing and the word preached.

Lutheran worship confessed consubstantiation in the Supper.

It kept the normative principle, retaining images and ceremonies.

Usage

"Honour Luther's recovery of the gospel, yet test his worship by the command of God, not the leave of man."

"Lutheran worship warns that a half-reformation in worship leaves the leaven of Rome behind."

"The regulative principle teaches that what God has not commanded in His worship, He has forbidden."
